Red blood cells in hyperadrenalinemia

One rat experiment found no significant red-cell change after one hour but reported improvement in several measures after 24 hours. The finding has not been replicated or tested in people.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Near-infrared exposure produced a delayed improvement in selected red-cell measures in a rat model of adrenaline-induced stress. The evidence is limited to one experiment and does not establish a clinical effect.

Summary of the Evidence

A single rat experiment reported improvement after 24 hours in red-cell morphology, membrane-related measures, osmotic resistance, and circulating cell count. The one-hour assessment was null, and no independent replication or human study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No study has tested PBM in people with hyperadrenalinemia. A broader narrative review of PBM and red-cell physiology includes this animal finding within a mixed preclinical literature but does not add clinical evidence for adrenaline-associated red-cell changes (Liebert et al. 2022).

Animal evidence

Rats received adrenaline before light was applied to the occipital region. PBM did not significantly change red-cell measures after one hour. At 24 hours, the treated group had fewer pathological red-cell forms, restored phase-portrait patterns, higher electrophoretic mobility and osmotic resistance, and a circulating red-cell count closer to intact animals (Deryugina et al. 2019).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The experiment used pulsed 890-nm near-infrared light at 415 Hz for ten minutes, with an average power density of 193 μW/cm² at the output window. One exposure in one stress model cannot define a treatment protocol for people or other red-cell disorders.

Interpretation

The study supports a delayed biological response in selected rat red-cell measures. Because the evidence is one preclinical experiment with no clinical outcomes, the result remains preliminary.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for adrenaline-associated red-cell changes in rats.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The evidence is one rat experiment with no independent replication or human outcomes. Changes appeared after 24 hours rather than at the one-hour assessment and concern red-cell morphology and physical properties, not symptoms or clinical benefit.
